title: Why Do We Age? The Evolution of Decay
question: If natural selection favors survival, why has it not eliminated aging?
summary: Aging looks like a flaw evolution should have fixed. The answer is that selection's power fades with age, leaving bodies tuned for reproduction rather than endurance.
content:
The Puzzle

Natural selection sharpens organisms for survival and reproduction, yet nearly every complex animal deteriorates with time. Some species barely seem to: certain tortoises, rockfish and the Greenland shark show little actuarial decline, and the hydra appears effectively non-aging. So aging is neither physically inevitable nor universal. It is something evolution allowed.

The Shadow of Selection

Peter Medawar's insight in the 1950s was that selection weakens with age. In the wild, most animals die from predators, disease or hunger long before senescence sets in. A gene that harms you at age 90 is almost never expressed in the wild, so selection cannot see it. Mutations with late-acting damage accumulate quietly in the genome, like debris in a place no one sweeps.

Trade-offs: Antagonistic Pleiotropy

George Williams added a sharper idea: some genes help when young and harm when old. A gene boosting early fertility or rapid growth will spread even if it causes cancer or arterial stiffening decades later. Aging, then, is partly the bill for youthful vigor. Calcium deposition that builds strong bones in youth may calcify arteries in age.

The Disposable Soma

Tom Kirkwood framed this as economics. Energy can go to reproduction or to repair. Perfect maintenance is costly, and an animal likely to die of accident soon is better off investing in offspring. This predicts that species facing high external mortality should age faster, which broadly holds: mice live two years, bats of similar size can live over thirty, and island opossums that escaped predators evolved slower aging.

Mechanisms Beneath the Theory

At the cellular level, aging involves damage accumulation: telomere shortening, mutations, misfolded proteins, mitochondrial dysfunction, senescent cells that refuse to die and secrete inflammatory signals. Pathways such as insulin/IGF-1 and mTOR link nutrition to lifespan; caloric restriction extends life in many species. Evolutionary theory says why; molecular biology says how.

Can It Be Changed?

If aging is a set of tunable trade-offs rather than a hard law, interventions become conceivable: clearing senescent cells, modulating mTOR, partial cellular reprogramming. Whether these can add healthy years without paying the pleiotropic price evolution warns about remains open.

perspectives.title: Evolutionary Biology
perspectives.description: Aging is not selected for but tolerated: the force of selection declines with age, so late-life harms go unchecked and trade-offs favor early reproduction.

perspectives.title: Cell Biology
perspectives.description: Aging is accumulated molecular damage and failing maintenance: telomere erosion, senescent cells, protein aggregation and mitochondrial decline.

perspectives.title: Medicine
perspectives.description: Treating age itself as the root risk factor for cancer, dementia and heart disease reframes disease-by-disease medicine as geroscience.

perspectives.title: Philosophy
perspectives.description: Does death give life meaning, or is that a consoling story we tell about a biological accident? Extending life raises questions of identity, inequality and purpose.
